text: Theorem. Let \(Q\) be a finite \(3\)-group of class \(\le4\) with \(\gamma_4(Q)^3=1\). Then \(D_5(Q)=1\). More generally, \(D_5(G)=\gamma_5(G)\) for every group \(G\) such that \(G/\gamma_2(G)\) is a finite \(3\)-group and \(\gamma_4(G)^3\subseteq\gamma_5(G)\).

text: There is no condition on the exponents of \(Q/\gamma_2\), \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) or \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\). Theorems 6.9 and 6.10 are special cases: Theorem 6.10 is the case with, in addition, \(\gamma_2^9\subseteq\gamma_4\), and Theorem 6.9 is contained in it (see after Theorem 6.10). In particular, the obstruction \(\psi\ne0\) described after Theorem 6.10 is not an obstruction to \(D_5=1\). The difference with the proof of Theorem 6.10 is that the rows of (E) are not paired with \(x_i\) one at a time but summed over all \(i\): then the term \([R_i,Y_i]\) of each row cancels against the \(v\)-part by (F\(_2\)) (Lemma 2 below), and for the rows \(j\in N_9\) the inclusion \(R_j^{-9}\in\gamma_4\), which needed (H2), is not used. The result is an exact identity \((\star)\) for \(2g\), valid in every finite \(3\)-group of class \(\le4\).

text: (1) Identities. Let \(a,b\in\gamma_2\), \(c\in\gamma_3\) and \(x,y\in Q\); no condition on \(\gamma_4\) is assumed. (K1) \(a\mapsto[a,x]\) and \(c\mapsto[c,x]\) are homomorphisms \(\gamma_2\to\gamma_3\) and \(\gamma_3\to\gamma_4\) (as (I1) and (I2) in the proof of Theorem 6.10); \((a,b)\mapsto[a,b]\) is a bilinear map \(\gamma_2\times\gamma_2\to\gamma_4\) that depends only on \(\bar a,\bar b\in L_2\); we write it \(\omega(\bar a,\bar b)\). (K2) \([x^n,y]=c^n[c,x]^{\binom n2}[c,x,x]^{\binom n3}\) for \(c=[x,y]\) and \(n\ge1\). Indeed, \([x^n,y]=c^{x^{n-1}}\dotsm c^xc\) and \(c^{x^k}=c\,[c,x]^k[c,x,x]^{\binom k2}\), as \([c,x,x]\in\gamma_4\) is central and \([c,x,x,x]\in\gamma_5=1\); moreover \(c\) commutes with \([c,x]\in\gamma_3\). (K3) \([a,x^n]=[a,x]^n[a,x,x]^{\binom n2}\): by (K2) for the pair \((x,a)\), where now \([[x,a],x,x]\in\gamma_5=1\), and (K1). In particular, if \(\gamma_4^3=1\) and \(3\mid n\), then \([a,x^n]=[a,x]^n\). (K4) \(t(\bar a;\bar x,\bar y)=[a,x,y]\in\gamma_4\) depends only on \(\bar a\in L_2\) and \(\bar x,\bar y\in Q_{ab}\), and is trilinear. Since \([c,y^m]=[c,y]^m\) for \(c\in\gamma_3\), we have \(t(\cdot\,;\bar x,\bar y)^m=1\) if \(y^m\in\gamma_2\), and also if \(x^m\in\gamma_2\) (by (K3), as \([a,x^m]\in\gamma_4\) and \(\binom m2[a,x,x,y]=0\)). (K5) \([a,x,y]-[a,y,x]=\omega(\bar a,[\bar x,\bar y])\) in \(\gamma_4\) (the Hall–Witt identity in class \(\le4\)).

text: (2) Tahara's conditions. Let \(x_1,\dots,x_s\) be a basis of uniqueness of \(Q_{ab}\) with orders \(d(i)\) (it is chosen in step (4)), and let \(x_{2k}\), \(x_{3l}\) be bases of uniqueness of \(L_2\), \(L_3\) with orders \(e(k)\), \(f(l)\), all powers of \(3\) larger than \(1\). The constants \(b_{hk}\), \(c_{hl}\), \(d_{kl}\), \(\alpha^{(gh)}_l\) and \(\bar y_h\) are as in the proof of Theorem 6.10; \(Y_i=x_i^{d(i)}\), \(q_{ij}=d(j)/d(i)\), and we put \(c_{ij}=[x_i,x_j]\). By [Tah81, Thm. 6.1], \(D_5(Q)\) is generated by the elements \(g=U+V+W\in\gamma_3\), \[U=\sum_{i<j}u_{ij}q_{ij}[Y_i,x_j]=\sum_{i<j}u_{ij}[x_i^{d(j)},x_j], V=\sum_{i,k}v_{ik}\sum_{l>k}b_{il}[x_{2l},x_{2k}],\qquad W=\sum_{i\le j\le k}w_{ijk}[Y_i,x_j,x_k]\] (the second form of \(U\) by (K1), as \(q_{ij}[Y_i,x_j]=[Y_i^{q_{ij}},x_j]\)), over the integer families \(\tau=(u,v,v',w,w',w'')\) satisfying (A)–(F). We use only (B) and (E), written out in the proof of Theorem 6.10, and the following parts of (C), (D), (F) (the subscripts are those of the formalization): (C\(_1\)) \(u_{ij}q_{ij}\binom{d(i)}3+w_{iij}\binom{d(i)}2\equiv0\pmod{d(i)}\) for \(i<j\); (D\(_2\)) \(\sum_{h\le i}w_{hij}b_{hk}+\sum_{i<h\le j}w'_{ihj}b_{hk}+\sum_{h>j}w''_{ijh}b_{hk}\equiv0\pmod{(d(i),e(k))}\) for \(i<j\) and every \(k\); (F\(_2\)) \(\sum_iv_{ik}b_{il}+\sum_iv_{il}b_{ik}\equiv0\pmod{e(k)}\) for \(k<l\).

text: Lemma 1 (a row of (E)). \(U_i=d(i)[R_i,x_i]+\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}[Y_h,x_i]-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}q_{hi}[Y_h,x_i,x_i]-\langle E^w_i,x_i\rangle\). Indeed, the derivation of \((\ast)\) in the proof of Theorem 6.10 uses only (B), (E) and class \(\le4\), neither (H1) nor (H2); so \(R_i^{-d(i)}Z_i\in\gamma_3\) satisfies \((\ast)\). We pair \((\ast)\) with \(x_i\), that is, apply \(c\mapsto[c,x_i]\) (K1), which kills \(\gamma_4\). For each \(l\) the order of \([x_{3l},x_i]\) divides \(f(l)\), as \(x_{3l}^{f(l)}\in\gamma_4\), and divides \(d(i)\), as \([x_{3l},x_i]^{d(i)}=[x_{3l},Y_i]=1\) by (K4) and \([\gamma_3,\gamma_2]=1\); so the multiples of \((d(i),f(l))\) allowed in \((\ast)\) contribute nothing, whatever the exponent of \(\gamma_4\). As \([Y_h,x_i]\equiv\prod_lx_{3l}^{\alpha^{(hi)}_l}\pmod{\gamma_4}\), we get \[[R_i^{-d(i)}Z_i,x_i]=-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}q_{hi}[Y_h,x_i,x_i]-\langle E^w_i,x_i\rangle,\] and by (K1) the left side is \(-d(i)[R_i,x_i]-\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}[Y_h,x_i]+U_i\).

text: Lemma 2. \(d(i)[R_i,x_i]=[R_i,Y_i]-\binom{d(i)}2[R_i,x_i,x_i]\), and \(\sum_i[R_i,Y_i]+2V=0\). The first is (K3). For the second, let \(\omega_{kl}=[x_{2k},x_{2l}]\). As \(\bar Y_i=\sum_lb_{il}\bar x_{2l}\) in \(L_2\), \([R_i,Y_i]=\sum_{k,l}v_{ik}b_{il}\omega_{kl}=\sum_{k<l}(v_{il}b_{ik}-v_{ik}b_{il})\omega_{lk}\), while the row \(i\) of \(V\) is \(V_i=\sum_{k<l}v_{ik}b_{il}\omega_{lk}\). So \([R_i,Y_i]+2V_i=\sum_{k<l}(v_{ik}b_{il}+v_{il}b_{ik})\omega_{lk}\). Summed over \(i\), the coefficient of \(\omega_{lk}\) is divisible by \(e(k)\) by (F\(_2\)), and \(\omega_{lk}^{e(k)}=[x_{2l},x_{2k}^{e(k)}]=1\), as \(x_{2k}^{e(k)}\in\gamma_3\).

text: Lemma 3. \[2W-\sum_i\langle E^w_i,x_i\rangle =-\sum_{i<g\le h}w'_{igh}[Y_g,x_i,x_h]-\sum_{j<k<h}w''_{jkh}\,\omega(\bar Y_h,\bar c_{jk}).\] Pairing \(E^w_i\) with \(x_i\) and summing over \(i\), the three sums of \(E^w_{il}\) give \(\sum_{g\le i\le h}w_{gih}[Y_g,x_h,x_i]\), \(\sum_{g\le h\le i}w_{ghi}[Y_g,x_h,x_i]=W\) and \(\sum_{i<g\le h}w'_{igh}[Y_g,x_h,x_i]\). So the left side equals \[\sum_{g\le j\le k}w_{gjk}([Y_g,x_j,x_k]-[Y_g,x_k,x_j])-\sum_{i<g\le h}w'_{igh}[Y_g,x_h,x_i],\] and the bracket is \(\omega(\bar Y_g,\bar c_{jk})\) by (K5), which vanishes for \(j=k\). Multiply (D\(_2\)) for a pair \(j<k\) and the column \(m\) by \(\omega(\bar x_{2m},\bar c_{jk})\) and sum over \(m\). The modulus \((d(j),e(m))\) does not matter, since \(e(m)\bar x_{2m}=0\) and \(d(j)\bar c_{jk}=[d(j)\bar x_j,\bar x_k]=0\) in \(L_2\); and \(\sum_mb_{hm}\bar x_{2m}=\bar Y_h\). This gives \[\sum_{h\le j}w_{hjk}\,\omega(\bar Y_h,\bar c_{jk}) =-\sum_{j<h\le k}w'_{jhk}\,\omega(\bar Y_h,\bar c_{jk})-\sum_{h>k}w''_{jkh}\,\omega(\bar Y_h,\bar c_{jk}).\] We substitute this; the terms with \(w'\) combine by (K5): \(\omega(\bar Y_g,\bar c_{ih})+[Y_g,x_h,x_i]=[Y_g,x_i,x_h]\).

text: Proposition \((\star)\). For every family \(\tau\) satisfying (B), (D\(_2\)), (E) and (F\(_2\)), in every finite \(3\)-group of class \(\le4\), \[\begin{split}2g={} \underbrace{\sum_{i<h}u_{ih}\Delta_{ih}}_{T_1}\ \underbrace{-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}q_{hi}[Y_h,x_i,x_i]}_{T_2}\ \underbrace{-\sum_{i<g\le h}w'_{igh}[Y_g,x_i,x_h]}_{T_3} \underbrace{-\sum_{j<k<h}w''_{jkh}[Y_h,c_{jk}]}_{T_4}\ \underbrace{-\sum_i\tbinom{d(i)}2[R_i,x_i,x_i]}_{T_5},\end{split}\tag{$\star$}\] where \(\Delta_{ih}=[x_i^{d(h)},x_h]+[x_h^{d(h)},x_i]\). Indeed, \(2U=U+\sum_iU_i\); by Lemmas 1 and 2, \(\sum_iU_i=\sum_i[R_i,Y_i]+T_5+\sum_{i<h}u_{ih}[x_h^{d(h)},x_i]+T_2-\sum_i\langle E^w_i,x_i\rangle\), and adding \(U=\sum_{i<h}u_{ih}[x_i^{d(h)},x_h]\) gives \(T_1\). Then \(\sum_i[R_i,Y_i]+2V=0\) by Lemma 2, and \(2W-\sum_i\langle E^w_i,x_i\rangle=T_3+T_4\) by Lemma 3, as \(\omega(\bar Y_h,\bar c_{jk})=[Y_h,c_{jk}]\). Conditions (A), (C), (D\(_1\)), (F\(_1\)) are not used here.

text: The defect \(\Delta\). Let \(i<h\), \(n=d(h)\) and \(c=c_{ih}\), so \([x_h,x_i]=c^{-1}\). By (K2) for both terms, \(\Delta_{ih}=\binom n2([c,x_i]-[c,x_h])+\binom n3([c,x_i,x_i]-[c,x_h,x_h])\), and by (K3) \(n[c,x]=[c,x^n]-\binom n2[c,x,x]\), where \([c,x_i^n]=q_{ih}\,\omega(\bar c,\bar Y_i)\) and \([c,x_h^n]=\omega(\bar c,\bar Y_h)\). As \(n\) is odd, \[\Delta_{ih}=\tfrac{n-1}2\bigl(q_{ih}\,\omega(\bar c,\bar Y_i)-\omega(\bar c,\bar Y_h)\bigr)-\tfrac{n(n^2-1)}{12}\bigl(t(\bar c;\bar x_i,\bar x_i)-t(\bar c;\bar x_h,\bar x_h)\bigr),\tag{$\Delta$}\] and \(d(i)\bar c=0\) in \(L_2\), so \(\omega(\bar c,\cdot)\) and \(t(\bar c;\cdot)\) are killed by \(d(i)\).

text: (4) \(g=1\) when \(\gamma_4^3=1\). We choose the basis \(x_1,\dots,x_s\) as in the proofs of Theorems 6.9 and 6.10, adapted to the heights and to \(K\) only. By (I7) of the proof of Theorem 6.10, which uses only the Hall–Petrescu formula, the cube map induces a linear map \(\bar P\colon V\to L_2/3L_2\) on \(V=\{\bar x\in Q_{ab}:3\bar x=0\}\); let \(K=\ker\bar P\). The claim in the proof of Theorem 6.9 (with this \(\bar P\)) gives a basis \(z_1,\dots,z_s\) of \(V\) such that every \(V_j=V\cap3^jQ_{ab}\) and every \(V_j\cap K\) is spanned by a subset of it, and as there we obtain a basis of uniqueness \(x_1,\dots,x_s\) of \(Q_{ab}\) with orders \(d(1)\le\dots\le d(s)\) and \(\bar Y_i+3L_2=\bar P(z_i)\). Let \(N=\{i:z_i\in K\}\) and \(A=\{i:z_i\notin K\}\). Then \(\bar Y_i\in3L_2\) for \(i\in N\), and the classes of \(\bar Y_h\), \(h\in A\), in \(L_2/3L_2\) are linearly independent. The bases \(x_{2k}\), \(x_{3l}\) are arbitrary. Modulo \(3\): (c1) \(3\mid u_{ij}\) if \(i<j\) and \(d(i)=d(j)\): by (C\(_1\)), as \(v_3\binom d3=v_3(d)-1\) and \(v_3\binom d2=v_3(d)\) for a power \(d\ge3\) of \(3\). (c2) \(3\mid u_{ih}\) if \(i<h\) and \(h\in A\): as \(3\) divides \(d(i)\) and \(e(k)\), (B) for the row \(i\) gives \(\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}\bar Y_h-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}q_{hi}\bar Y_h\in3L_2\); the terms with \(h\in N\) lie in \(3L_2\), and the classes of the \(\bar Y_h\), \(h\in A\), are independent modulo \(3L_2\). (c3) \(3\mid w'_{igh}\) if \(g\in A\), and \(3\mid w''_{jkh}\) if \(h\in A\): in the same way from (D\(_2\)) for the pair \((i,h)\), respectively \((j,k)\), in which each index occurs in exactly one sum. Now every term of \((\star)\) vanishes, \(\gamma_4\) being of exponent \(3\): \(T_5\), since \(3\mid\binom{d(i)}2\). \(T_4\): for \(h\in A\) by (c3); for \(h\in N\), \(\bar Y_h=3\bar a\) with \(\bar a\in L_2\), and \(\omega(3\bar a,\cdot)=0\). \(T_3\): for \(g\in A\) by (c3); for \(g\in N\), \([Y_g,x_i,x_h]=t(3\bar a;\bar x_i,\bar x_h)=0\). \(T_2\): for \(d(h)<d(i)\), \(3\mid q_{hi}\); for \(d(h)=d(i)\), \(3\mid u_{hi}\) by (c1). \(T_1\), by \((\Delta)\) with \(n=d(h)\ge d(i)\) and \(\bar c=\bar c_{ih}\): the coefficient \(\tfrac{n(n^2-1)}{12}\) of the \(t\)-terms is divisible by \(3\) for \(n\ge9\), and for \(n=3\) we have \(d(i)=3\) and \(3\mid u_{ih}\) by (c1); the term \(q_{ih}\,\omega(\bar c,\bar Y_i)\) has \(3\mid q_{ih}\) if \(d(i)<n\), and \(3\mid u_{ih}\) by (c1) if \(d(i)=n\); the term \(\omega(\bar c,\bar Y_h)\) vanishes for \(h\in N\), as \(\bar Y_h\in3L_2\), and has \(3\mid u_{ih}\) for \(h\in A\), by (c2). So \(2g=0\) in \(\gamma_3\), a group of odd order; hence \(g=1\) for every admissible family, and \(D_5(Q)=1\) by [Tah81, Thm. 6.1].

text: Compared with the proof of Theorem 6.10: there the rows \(i\in A_3\) and \(j\in N_9\) were paired with \(x_i\), respectively \(x_j\), separately and the \(v\)-part was computed by hand, and the rows \(j\in N_9\) needed \(R_j^{-9}\in\gamma_4\), that is, (H2); here all rows are summed, and \(\sum_i[R_i,Y_i]\) cancels against \(2V\) by (F\(_2\)). Nor is the basis of \(L_2\) adapted to \(\bar P\), as it was there: only the independence of the \(\bar Y_h\), \(h\in A\), modulo \(3L_2\) is used. A computational check: identity \((\star)\) holds, on a basis of the lattice of families satisfying (B), (D), (E), (F), in \(1097\) random groups of class \(4\) with \(\gamma_4\) of exponent \(3\) or \(9\), \(Q_{ab}\) of types \([9,9]\), \([3,9,9]\), \([3,3,9,9]\), \([9,9,9]\), \([3,9,9,9]\), \([3,9,27]\), \([3,3,9,27]\), \([9,27]\), \([27,27]\), \([3,27,27]\) or \([3,3,27,27]\), of orders \(3^9\)–\(3^{91}\); and in the adapted basis every term \(T_1,\dots,T_5\), and \(g\), is trivial on a basis of the lattice of admissible families. Of these groups, \(436\) have \(\gamma_4^3=1\), among them \(139\) with \(\gamma_4\cong C_3\), cyclic centre and \(\gamma_2^9\not\subseteq\gamma_4\), to which Theorem 6.10 does not apply. As negative controls, \((\star)\) fails in \(318\), \(163\), \(434\) and \(130\) of the groups when (B), (D), (E) or (F), respectively, is dropped. text: Remark. [the case \(\gamma_4\cong C_9\)] Steps (1)–(3) of the proof of Theorem 6.11 do not use the exponent of \(\gamma_4\), so \((\star)\) and \((\Delta)\) hold in every finite \(3\)-group of class \(\le4\), and so do (c1)–(c3) for the basis of step (4). Let \(\gamma_4\) have exponent \(9\), for instance \(\gamma_4\cong C_9\). Then still \(T_5=0\), as \(d(i)\mid\binom{d(i)}2\) and \([R_i,x_i,x_i]^{d(i)}=[[R_i,x_i],Y_i]=1\) by (K4). Each argument of step (4) for \(T_1,\dots,T_4\) still gives a factor \(3\) in front of a value of \(\omega\) or \(t\), so these terms lie in \(\gamma_4^3\), and so does \(g\), in accordance with Corollary 6.12; but they need not vanish. The terms with an index of order \(3\) do vanish: the relevant value of \(\omega\) or \(t\) is then killed by \(3\) (for \(T_1\) with \(d(i)=3\) and \(T_4\) with \(d(j)=3\) because \(3\bar c=0\); for \(T_2\) with \(d(i)=3\) and \(T_3\) with \(d(i)=3\) by (K4)), and for \(T_2\) with \(d(h)=3\), \(d(i)=9\) one uses \([Y_h,x_i,x_i]=[c_{hi},x_i]^3\), from (K2), so that the term is \(-u_{hi}[c_{hi},x_i]^9=-u_{hi}\,\omega(\bar c_{hi},\bar Y_i)\) by (K3) (the \(t\)-term is killed by \(3\), as \(3\bar c_{hi}=0\)), which vanishes by (c2) if \(i\in A\) and as \(\bar Y_i\in3L_2\) if \(i\in N\) (for \(d(i)\ge27\), \(9\mid q_{hi}\)). What remains are terms \(3\cdot(\text{a value of }\omega\text{ or }t)\in\gamma_4^3\) (\(\cong C_3\) when \(\gamma_4\cong C_9\)) on generators \(x_i\) of order \(\ge9\) modulo \(\gamma_2\): \(T_1\) for \(9\le d(i)\le d(h)\), \(T_2\) for \(d(h)\ge9\), \(T_3\) for \(d(i)\ge9\), \(T_4\) for \(d(j)\ge9\). To kill them one would need information not used here, e.g. (A), (C\(_2\))–(C\(_4\)), (D\(_1\)), (F\(_1\)), (B) and (D\(_2\)) modulo \(9\), or the row \(h\) of (E) paired with other \(x_m\). Computations: in the \(661\) groups of the check after Theorem 6.11 with \(\gamma_4\) of exponent \(9\) (\(531\) of them with \(\gamma_4\cong C_9\) and cyclic centre) every term \(T_1,\dots,T_5\) is trivial on the lattice of admissible families in the adapted basis, which is more than is proved here. Independently, the truncated Magnus algebra (with the exactness certificate; the control \(z\in D_4\) holds in all) gives \(D_5=1\) in \(940\) random groups of class \(4\) with \(\gamma_4\cong C_9\), cyclic centre, \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) of exponent \(9\) or \(27\) and \(Q_{ab}\) of types \([9,9,3]\), \([9,9,3,3]\), \([9,9,9]\), \([9,9,9,3]\), \([27,9,3]\), \([27,9,3,3]\), \([27,27,3]\) or \([27,27,3,3]\), of orders \(3^{11}\)–\(3^{26}\), \(287\) of them with \(\gamma_2^9\not\subseteq\gamma_4\): the generator \(z\) of \(\Omega_1(Z)=\gamma_4^3\) does not lie in \(D_5\) (so \(D_5=1\), as a nontrivial normal subgroup meets the cyclic centre), and the solver of Tahara's conditions gives \(g=1\) in all of them. text: \(P\) has \(p\)-class \(3\), so it is nonterminal if and only if there is a group \(Q\) with a central subgroup \(\langle z\rangle\) of order \(p\), \(Q/\langle z\rangle\cong P\) and \(\gamma_4(Q)\ne1\). In such \(Q\) we have \(\gamma_4(Q)=\langle z\rangle\), \(\gamma_5(Q)=1\), \(Q''=1\) by Lemma 6.3, and \(\gamma_3(Q)\) of exponent \(p\); (N1)–(N3) follow. Write \(A=\gamma_2(Q)\) additively and \(D_xa=[a,x]\): the \(D_x\) commute on \(A\) and products of three of them vanish. Then the Hall–Witt identity becomes \([x,y,t]+[y,t,x]+[t,x,y]=0\) exactly, and its \(z\)-component on generators is (J). Comparing \((x_j^p)^{x_i}\) with \((x_j[x_j,x_i])^p\) gives (E). The unknowns are the exponents of \(z\) in \([v,x_i]=z^{\eta_i}\), \([u,x_i]=w^{f_i}z^{\sigma_i}\), \([w,x_i]=z^{cf_i}\), \(u^p=z^{\mu_u}\), \(v^p=z^{\mu_v}\). Conversely, a solution defines a pc-presentation on \(x_1,\dots,x_d,u,v,w,z\). Its consistency test words differ in the exponent of \(z\) by \(-J\), \(\pm E\) or \(0\), so it is consistent, and the group it defines has \(\gamma_4=\langle z\rangle\ne1\).

The two agree, and \(N\ne1\) exactly for the groups satisfying (N1)–(N4): \(190\), \(102\), \(110\), \(118\) groups. For each of these, the pc-presentation of the proof built from the solution was checked to be consistent, with \(\gamma_4\ne1\), and to map onto \(P\); so for these groups sufficiency does not rest on the consistency test. Without the term \(c\,\omega_3f\) in (J) the criterion gives wrong answers both ways: on the block it accepts \(295\) terminal groups and rejects \(13\) nonterminal ones. Code: compute/magnus. • The system is linear and homogeneous in \((c,\eta,\sigma,\mu_u,\mu_v)\), so (N4) is the solvability of an inhomogeneous linear system. The term with \(\varepsilon_p\) is \(\binom p3[x_j,x_i,x_j,x_j]\), the only place where \(p=3\) differs from \(p\ge5\). Whether (N4) holds does not depend on the choices made, since it is equivalent to nonterminality. • The criterion assumes \(P/\gamma_2\) elementary abelian, i.e. \(d(P)=d\); this implies that \(P\) has \(p\)-class \(3\), but not conversely.
